flashcards.q: What are the three layers of trust when evaluating a new model release, in order of increasing reliability?
flashcards.a: Layer 1: lab self-report (selected, incentive-biased). Layer 2: independent aggregator like Artificial Analysis or LM Arena (comparable, but still someone's methodology/weighting). Layer 3: your own eval on your task distribution (slow but the only one that answers your actual question).

flashcards.q: What is the single fastest tell that a launch benchmark comparison table is misleading?
flashcards.a: Count the blank/unpublished competitor cells. If a large fraction of a model's claimed 'wins' are against rows where the competitor's score was never published, the comparison is a marketing artifact, not an evaluation.

flashcards.q: In the Gemini 3.1 Pro 'won 13 of 16 benchmarks' launch claim (Feb 2026), what three things did the headline table not show?
flashcards.a: GPT-5.3-Codex's score was published for only 2 of 16 rows (most 'wins' were against blank cells); GDPval-AA showed Claude leading by roughly 300 Elo points, omitted from the table; and Humanity's Last Exam ranking flipped depending on tool-use condition, which wasn't surfaced in the summary.

flashcards.q: Why is MMLU no longer useful for discriminating among frontier models in 2026?
flashcards.a: Saturation (every serious frontier model scores in the low-to-mid 90s, compressing real differences below measurement noise) plus contamination (MMLU questions circulate publicly and leak into pretraining corpora, inflating scores independent of actual capability).

flashcards.q: How does date-stamped benchmarking (e.g. LiveCodeBench) defend against contamination?
flashcards.a: New problems are continuously harvested (from LeetCode, AtCoder, Codeforces) and annotated with a release date, so evaluation can be restricted to problems released strictly after a model's training cutoff, making contamination structurally impossible for that slice.

flashcards.q: What does the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.1 (June 2026) weight, by category?
flashcards.a: Agents 34% (incl. GDPval-AA v2, tau3-Banking), Coding 24% (incl. Terminal-Bench v2.1, SciCode), Scientific Reasoning 24% (incl. GPQA Diamond, CritPt), General 18% (incl. Humanity's Last Exam, AA-Omniscience hallucination benchmark).

flashcards.q: What does LM Arena Elo actually measure, and what is its documented manipulation vulnerability?
flashcards.a: Blind pairwise human preference converted to Elo via a Bradley-Terry fit -- a preference/popularity signal, not a correctness signal. Research (arXiv 2501.17858) showed coordinated voting with as few as a few hundred rigged votes, using output fingerprinting to identify a target model, can shift its ranking.

flashcards.q: What does METR's 'time horizon' metric measure, and how has its doubling rate changed?
flashcards.a: The length of task (measured in time a skilled human professional would take) a model can complete autonomously with 50% reliability. The doubling period compressed from roughly every 7 months (2019-2024) to roughly every 4 months (2024-2025). Measurements above ~16 hours are currently unreliable with METR's task suite.

flashcards.q: Compare Anthropic's RSP, OpenAI's Preparedness Framework, and Google DeepMind's FSF in one line each.
flashcards.a: Anthropic RSP: most prescriptive, ASL-1 through ASL-4+ with specific RAND weight-security-tier precommitments. OpenAI Preparedness: collapsed from four tiers to two qualitative bars (High/Critical), read by analysts as a weakening. Google FSF: most process-focused, specifies what will be measured/reviewed more than what action automatically follows.

flashcards.q: What regulatory milestone happened on 2 August 2026, and why does it matter?
flashcards.a: The EU AI Act's General-Purpose AI Code of Practice obligations began enforcement -- the first external enforcement mechanism on frontier model documentation and safety disclosure, as opposed to the three labs' voluntary, self-authored safety frameworks.

flashcards.q: What is the concrete licensing gotcha in Llama's license that a summary blog post typically undersells?
flashcards.a: A 700-million monthly-active-user cap measured at the parent corporate entity level, frozen at terms from a specific point in time rather than rolling forward, plus a separate exclusion of multimodal capabilities from the license grant specifically within the EU.

flashcards.q: Which open-weight model families use permissive MIT/Apache 2.0 licenses versus Llama's restrictive custom license?
flashcards.a: DeepSeek's V4 line (MIT), Qwen and Gemma (Apache 2.0) grant unrestricted commercial use, redistribution, and modification with no usage cap. Llama's custom license carries the 700M MAU cap and EU multimodal exclusion.

flashcards.q: What size of benchmark delta should be treated as noise rather than a real capability difference?
flashcards.a: Single-run accuracy deltas under roughly 2-3 points, and LM Arena Elo gaps under roughly 10 points, should be treated as ties until corroborated by repeated runs or a much larger sustained gap.

flashcards.q: What is the production-safe policy for adopting a new frontier model, versus 'always route to whatever tops the leaderboard'?
flashcards.a: Pin to a specific, immutable model version; migrate only after your own regression eval (on your task distribution, repeated runs) clears a stated bar, on a fixed review cadence -- never migrate the same day as a launch, since leaderboard rank reshuffles weekly and self-report/aggregator/Arena rankings frequently disagree.

flashcards.q: What's the structural difference between a model card and a system card?
flashcards.a: A model card documents the artifact (architecture, training data summary, context window, self-reported benchmarks). A system card documents the deployment (what tools/actions the model is wired to, what safeguards surround it, and the lab's own red-team findings, organized around risk categories like cyber, bio/chem uplift, persuasion, and model autonomy).
